events.headline: Oil Moves Higher on Rekindled War Fears

items.title: Oil Moves Higher on Rekindled War Fears

events.article_text:
What I Cover Irina Slav has been writing about global energy markets since 2007, covering the oil and gas industry, energy security, commodities, and the…

Crude oil prices started the week with a jump after President Trump rejected a peace deal proposal tabled by Iran last week at the UN General Assembly.

At the time of writing, Brent crude was trading at $107.24 per barrel, with West Texas Intermediate at $94.10 per barrel, the latter pressured by news that the U.S. federal government may institute a temporary ban on diesel, which would force refiners to cut run rates, boosting the availability of crude oil.

Interestingly, a fresh report about improving oil flows out of the Persian Gulf failed to offset fears of continued war in the region. Normally, such news would pressure oil prices immediately and keep them pressured, as evidenced by developments since March. This time, it seems war-related concerns are taking the upper hand.

These concerns are well justified. The Wall Street Journal reported this weekend that president Trump was considering a resumption in military strikes on Iran once the November midterms are over, strengthening the prospect of a prolonged war. This would in turn prolong the disruption on normal oil trade.

The U.S. and Iran appear to be stuck on their mutual conditions for peace. Iran has conditioned its agreement to a deal—and the reopening of Hormuz—on the U.S. lifting its naval blockade and oil sanctions, and unfreezing Iranian funds. The U.S., on the other hand, appears to believe economic pressure would eventually break Iran and has rejected the idea of lifting either the naval blockade or the earlier sanctions.

What seems to be infusing the situation with additional uncertainty is President Trump’s tendency to change his approach to Iran, often radically. Earlier this month, he said he expected the war to be over right after the November midterms. Later, he was reported to have warned he would restart strikes against Iran. According to unnamed government officials cited by the Wall Street Journal, the outcome of the midterms will also affect the U.S. president’s views of and decisions on the war.

analysis.tldr: Rising global crude oil prices mean imported fuel for India will likely get costlier, putting upward pressure on domestic inflation and putting a strain on the rupee.
the_story: Crude oil prices jumped at the start of the week after U.S. President Trump rejected a peace deal proposal tabled by Iran at the UN General Assembly.
At the time of writing, Brent crude (global benchmark for oil) traded at $107.24 per barrel, while West Texas Intermediate (U.S. benchmark) traded at $94.10 per barrel.
The Wall Street Journal reported that President Trump is considering resuming military strikes on Iran after the November midterms, raising fears of a prolonged war and trade disruptions.

The U.S. and Iran remain stuck: Iran demands the U.S. lift its naval blockade, drop oil sanctions, and unfreezing funds to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, while the U.S. rejects this in favor of continued economic pressure.
analysis.what_happened: Global oil prices rose because political tensions and the threat of renewed military conflict between the U.S. and Iran increased fears that oil supplies from the Middle East will be disrupted. President Trump rejected Iran's peace deal, and reports indicated potential military strikes could happen after November, keeping markets on edge despite some improving oil flows out of the Persian Gulf.
analysis.analogy: It is like a major grocery supplier warning that a route might get blocked by a security dispute, causing shopkeepers everywhere to panic-buy and push up prices immediately.
why_it_matters_india: Conflict risk rises in a key oil-producing region, pushing global crude oil prices higher.
India imports a vast majority of its crude oil needs, meaning higher global prices instantly translate to a larger national oil import bill.
A higher oil import bill forces India to buy more dollars to pay for oil, causing the rupee to weaken (each rupee buys fewer dollars).
Costlier crude feeds into domestic fuel, transport, and manufacturing costs, driving up overall inflation (the rate at which prices rise) and pinching household budgets.

impacts.rationale: Directly driven up by fears of prolonged conflict and blocked oil trade routes — bad for importing nations like India as it raises energy costs.
A stronger dollar demand to pay for pricier oil typically weakens the rupee, which is bad because it makes all imports like electronics and foreign travel more expensive.
Higher global oil costs ripple through transport and production, raising everyday prices — generally bad for ordinary consumers.
Global uncertainty and war fears drive investors worldwide toward safe assets like gold, which can be a double-edged sword for domestic buyers wanting to purchase jewelry.

watch_next: Developments regarding the U.S. midterms and statements from the White House about military strikes
Any official updates on the reopening or blockage of the Strait of Hormuz
analysis.caveats: If unexpected diplomatic breakthroughs occur or Middle East oil flows surge faster than anticipated, oil prices could reverse their gains quickly.

events.headline: Demand estimate of fertilizer for Rabi 2026-27 may be 2 LT higher

items.title: Demand estimate of fertilizer for Rabi 2026-27 may be 2 LT higher
items.summary: India plans a nearly 350 lakh-tonne fertilizer demand for Rabi 2026-27, with Urea leading, amid mixed monsoon impact and policy focus.

items.title: Demand estimate of fertilizer for Rabi 2026-27 may be 2 LT higher
items.summary: India plans a nearly 350 lakh-tonne fertilizer demand for Rabi 2026-27, with Urea leading, amid mixed monsoon impact and policy focus.

events.article_text:
The two-day Rabi conference is likely to finalise the fertilizer demand after consultations with States

The government is set to estimate a demand of nearly 350 lakh tonnes (lt) of fertilisers – Urea, DAP, MOP and Complex (mix of nutrients N, P, K, S) for ensuing Rabi season starting from October 1, which is 2 lt higher from year-ago level, even as during Kharif season sales were below expectation amid drought declared in many tehsils (talukas) in Karnataka and Maharashtra.

The two-day Rabi conference, which begins from September 28, is likely to finalise the fertilizer demand after consultations with States, sources said. However, a month-wise preliminary estimate has been made of the requirement of these subsidised fertilizers during October 2026-March 2027, based on the feedback from the States, the sources added.

According to the estimate, the Urea demand has been pegged at 199.27 lt, that of DAP at 55.07 lt, MOP 16.4 lt and Complex 79.12 lt. Against this, the closing stock of fertilizer in the country as on September 18 was 141.69 lt — 64.91 lt Urea, 22.83 lt DAP, 9.38 lt MOP and 44.57 lt Complex.

As fertilizer demand is related to rainfall, particularly in rain-fed areas and to some extent in the canal irrigated land, due to 20 per cent lower than normal rainfall till during September 1-23, the sales of fertilizers also dropped. However, due to low pressure and deep depression, there was heavy rainfall after that which experts said could boost demand particularly in those pockets where there was precipitation.

Official data show that sales of Urea were 13.15 lt, DAP 4.39 lt, MOP 0.81 lt and Complex 3.25 lt during September 4-18. Against the monthly demand for whole of September estimated 54.48 lt – 26.77 lt Urea, 10.2 lt DAP, 2.87 lt MOP and 14.64 lt Complex — sales were only 21.6 lt or less than 40 per cent in 15 days for which data are available.

Meanwhile, the Department of Agriculture & Farmers’ Welfare on Sunday said that the annual Rabi Conference will bring together State Agriculture Ministers, senior officials of the Central and State Governments, ICAR and other stakeholders to deliberate on key priorities and preparedness for the season.

The conference will focus on strengthening Centre-State coordination and evolving a coordinated, outcome-oriented strategy for enhancing agricultural production, productivity, sustainability and farmers’ incomes. Fertilizer availability and balanced use of fertilizers among many other issues will be discussed on September 29.

Key issues to be deliberated upon will include the Mission for Aatmanirbharta in Pulses, oilseeds and oil palm, horticulture, cotton, seed availability and reforms in the seed value chain, natural farming, soil health, farm mechanisation, FPO financing and infrastructure, marketing reforms, PM Dhan-Dhaanya Krishi Yojana, Kisan Credit Card coverage, Digital Agriculture, PM Fasal Bima Yojana, plant protection and agricultural statistics, it said.

analysis.tldr: A higher government estimate for upcoming fertilizer demand means the national subsidy bill could swell, which matters for the government's fiscal health and farming input costs.
the_story: The government is set to estimate a demand of nearly 350 lakh tonnes of fertilizers (Urea, DAP, MOP, and Complex) for the upcoming Rabi season starting October 1, which is 2 lakh tonnes higher than last year.
A two-day Rabi conference beginning September 28 will finalise this demand after consulting with states, following preliminary month-wise estimates for October 2026 to March 2027.
Specific demand breakdowns include 199.27 lakh tonnes for Urea, 55.07 lakh tonnes for DAP, 16.4 lakh tonnes for MOP, and 79.12 lakh tonnes for Complex fertilizers.

Fertilizer sales dropped recently due to rainfall being 20 percent below normal between September 1-23, though subsequent heavy rainfall from low pressure and deep depression could boost demand in those pockets.
analysis.what_happened: The government is projecting a slight increase in fertilizer demand for the upcoming Rabi farming season starting October 1, reaching nearly 350 lakh tonnes. This preliminary projection is based on feedback from states, set to be finalized at the upcoming Rabi conference, even though recent sales slowed down due to erratic rainfall across various regions.
analysis.analogy: It is like a large household stocking up on extra groceries before a big family gathering, making sure they buy enough staples ahead of time so no one runs short.
why_it_matters_india: Higher estimated fertilizer demand requires the government to procure and supply more subsidized inputs to farmers.
An increased requirement for subsidised fertilizers can raise the overall government subsidy bill, affecting national finances.
Changes in fertilizer availability and usage directly impact farming productivity and rural incomes across states.
Discussions at the Rabi conference also touch on related rural priorities like Kisan Credit Card coverage and crop insurance schemes.

impacts.target: Fertilizer stocks like Coromandel International & Rashtriya Chemicals and Fertilizers (RCF)
impacts.rationale: Higher projected demand estimates can improve sales volume expectations for fertilizer manufacturing companies, which is generally good for their business revenue.
A higher total volume of subsidized fertilizer required by farmers increases the government's subsidy payout, which can strain public finances.

watch_next: Final outcomes and policy decisions from the two-day Rabi conference starting September 28
Actual progress of fertilizer sales as the Rabi season kicks off on October 1
analysis.caveats: Actual fertilizer consumption could differ from preliminary estimates if unexpected weather shifts or subsequent rainfall patterns alter farmers' field requirements.

events.headline: RBI likely to cap interest rate hikes at 25 - 50 bps , inflation could ease in 2027 : Report

items.title: RBI likely to cap interest rate hikes at 25 - 50 bps , inflation could ease in 2027 : Report

events.article_text:
New Delhi, Sep 28 (IANS) The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) is likely to limit its interest rate increases to 25-50 basis points in the current cycle with markets pricing in a more aggressive tightening path than warranted, according to a report.

Analysts at global brokerage Nomura assigned an 80 per cent probability to a limited recalibration cycle rather than a broader tightening cycle involving more than 75 basis points of rate hikes.

Markets are currently pricing close to 125 basis points of rate increases over the next year, which Nomura said was excessive given the current inflation dynamics.

However, the central bank could raise its policy rate by 25 basis points each in October and December, taking the terminal rate to 5.75 per cent, according to the brokerage.

Moreover, it also sees some risk of a single rate hike.

The probability of further rate increases is expected to diminish from February 2027 as consumption could slow and the year-ahead inflation outlook improves, according to the report.

The current disinflationary trend differed from the 2016-17 period with the latest moderation driven significantly by lower core inflation. Core inflation has fallen from around 5 per cent to about 3 per cent, it added.

"Given limited signs of generalisation, a tightening cycle is unlikely," Nomura said. It also stated that a pre-emptive rate hike could be appropriate to keep inflation expectations anchored.

Food prices remain the main near-term risk to the inflation outlook, although government supply-side measures could help contain some price pressures.

It expects headline consumer price inflation to ease around 5.3 per cent in the first half of 2027.

Additionally, inflation is expected to fall below 4 per cent in the second half of 2027, while adverse base effects could add about 0.8 per cent to headline inflation in October-November.

For the full financial year, Nomura forecasts CPI inflation at 5.2 per cent in FY27 and 4 per cent in FY28. While core CPI inflation is projected at 4.3 per cent and 4 per cent, respectively.

analysis.tldr: Loans may not become as expensive as people fear, because a major report says the RBI (Reserve Bank of India, the country's central bank) will likely keep interest rate increases small.
the_story: Global brokerage Nomura predicts the RBI will limit its total interest rate increases to 25-50 basis points (where 100 basis points equals 1 percentage point) in this cycle.
Nomura assigns an 80 percent probability to this limited rate path, stating that financial markets are incorrectly expecting a much harsher hike of up to 125 basis points.
The RBI could raise its policy rate by 25 basis points each in October and December, pushing the final peak rate to 5.75 percent.
Price rises (inflation) are expected to ease later, falling below 4 percent in the second half of 2027 as consumption slows down.
analysis.what_happened: The brokerage firm Nomura released a report analyzing the RBI's next moves. They found that regular markets are panicking and expecting massive interest rate hikes, but actual economic data shows inflation is cooling down, meaning the central bank won't need to raise borrowing costs heavily.
analysis.analogy: It is like a doctor prescribing a mild medicine because your fever is already going down by itself, even though your anxious family members want you to take a much stronger dose.
why_it_matters_india: Nomura predicts smaller interest rate hikes by the RBI -> banks do not raise loan rates as aggressively as feared -> home and car loan EMIs (Equated Monthly Installments, fixed monthly loan payments) stay more manageable for borrowers.

Core inflation (prices of manufactured goods and services excluding food and fuel) drops from 5 percent to about 3 percent -> price pressures generalise less -> the RBI feels less pressure to keep punishing the economy with high rates.
Food prices remain a short-term risk -> government steps in with supply measures -> prevents food inflation from spiraling out of control.

Inflation expectations stabilize -> headline consumer price inflation (overall measure of the cost of living for households) drops below 4 percent by late 2027 -> purchasing power of ordinary citizens gets protected over the long run.

impacts.target: Interest rates on home and car loans
impacts.rationale: Small increases of 25 to 50 basis points are still expected soon, meaning your loan costs will edge up slightly, but not as brutally as markets feared — good news for keeping borrowing affordable.

Core inflation has already dropped significantly to 3 percent and overall inflation is projected to ease to 4 percent by late 2027, meaning the cost of living pressures will eventually cool down for families.

impacts.target: 10-year bond yield (interest India pays to borrow)
impacts.rationale: Since the RBI is expected to stop raising rates sooner than markets feared, government borrowing costs will settle down, which generally keeps broader market interest rates lower.

watch_next: Actual RBI announcements in October and December regarding the policy rate
Near-term food price changes and government supply measures
Monthly consumer price inflation (CPI) data releases
analysis.caveats: If food prices spike unexpectedly or adverse base effects push inflation up severely in October-November, the RBI might be forced to abandon this gentle path and hike rates more aggressively.

events.headline: India's golden data centre opportunity: Policymakers can make the most of it by ensuring regulatory certainty

items.title: India's golden data centre opportunity: Policymakers can make the most of it by ensuring regulatory certainty
items.summary: The assumption that investors are making a beeline for Indian locations is misplaced. Global capital is exceptionally mobile and India is one of many options for new capacities. Regulation predictability is what the country must offer global investors to lure investment in digital set-ups

events.article_text:
India’s aspiration to become a data centre hub is underpinned by a simple economic reality. Few countries generate data at India’s scale. Fewer still combine that scale with a large domestic market, growing cloud adoption, a huge talent pool and an increasingly important role in AI-driven services. Yet, India’s share of global data centre capacity remains modest.

Data generation and data centre investment do not necessarily converge. Nations that generate vast quantities of data would appear to be natural locations for the digital infrastructure that stores, processes and derives value from that data. Yet, data availability alone is rarely sufficient to attract large-scale investment.

The differentiating factor is often not the incentives on offer, but the degree of regulatory certainty. Data centres sit at the intersection of multiple regulatory regimes. The issue is not over-regulation, but fragmentation. A hyperscale data processing facility may need to navigate telecom regulation, cybersecurity requirements, power sector rules, environment approvals (including for efficient water usage), data governance obligations and tax considerations.

All these regulatory obligations are handled by different agencies and processes. A common feature among jurisdictions that have attracted significant investments is greater transparency and convergence, not necessarily lighter regulation.

Take Ireland. Faced with concerns about grid capacity and energy consumption, it has introduced a series of measures governing large energy users, including data centres.

These measures are neither liberal nor concessional. However, they are accompanied by detailed policy frameworks that define the conditions under which future data centre development will be accommodated, allowing investors to evaluate projects against a firm regulatory backdrop. The goal is to make the regulatory pathway easier to navigate by making it transparent, simple and, most importantly, predictable.

Data governance presents a slightly different challenge. India permits participation in global digital ecosystems; indeed, the current framework is considerably more open than most businesses had anticipated.

The more relevant questions arise at the margins: how India’s data-protection framework interacts with sector-specific localization requirements, how future restrictions on cross-border data transfers may evolve, and how businesses operating across multiple jurisdictions can navigate overlapping regulatory obligations.

These questions are particularly important for cloud providers, global capability centres and AI-driven businesses whose operating models are inherently cross-border. As investments grow larger, tax predictability also gains importance.

The critical question is whether India can offer regulatory certainty for long-term digital infrastructure investments. Recent policy measures reveal an encouraging trend. The ministry of finance has announced a 21-year tax carve-out for certain foreign cloud service providers that use Indian data centre infrastructure to serve overseas markets.

This responds to investor demand that the mere use of Indian infrastructure should not trigger additional layers of taxation.

The success of such moves, however, will depend not only on the statutory exemption itself, but also on adherence to its underlying rationale. This should be clearly reflected in subordinate regulations, as delays in enforcement does not bode well for investor confidence. Clarity in legislation could avoid negative outcomes due to overzealous enforcement. As always, the devil lies in the details. So the ministry’s effort to engage with the industry signifies a welcome consultative approach.

Cloud providers may be willing to accept taxation where economic activity occurs, but may be less comfortable with it where the availability of an infrastructure-focused concession is contingent on the adoption of a particular commercial distribution model. Thus, the new law’s requirement that cloud services to Indian users be supplied only through Indian resellers may discourage potential investors.

Tax incentives are generally most effective when they provide clear outcomes without influencing commercial decisions and should remain agnostic to business models. A condition that effectively prescribes how cloud providers must structure customer-facing sales arrangements risks introducing an additional layer of regulatory complexity into the investment calculus. This may dilute the India’s attractiveness as a global hub for data centres.

If India wishes to attract long-term investments in cloud and AI infrastructure, as the country’s political leadership has clearly signalled, it is critical that the spirit of such tax carve-outs is preserved in all subordinate regulations and related measures.

From our long experience of being able to attract less than 10% of global capital flows, we must learn the lesson that global capital is exceptionally mobile and India is but one of the options for it to locate new capacities. This applies not just to data centres, but other sectors as well.

Foreign investors are likely to favour jurisdictions that provide clear, consistent and constructive answers to regulatory and tax issues. The assumption that investors are making a beeline for Indian locations is misplaced; the sooner it is jettisoned, the better.

Seema Kejriwal, partner at BMR Legal, contributed to this article. These are the authors’ personal views.

The authors are, respectively, chairman, Pahle India Foundation, and former vice chairman, Niti Aayog; and partner, BMR Legal.

analysis.tldr: Clearer rules and predictable taxes for data centres could attract massive foreign tech investments, boosting India's digital economy and infrastructure stocks.
the_story: India has massive data generation, a huge talent pool, and a growing domestic market, but its share of global data centre capacity remains modest.
Data centres must navigate fragmented rules across telecom, cybersecurity, power, environment, and tax agencies, making regulatory certainty more important than financial incentives.
The Ministry of Finance offered a 21-year tax carve-out for certain foreign cloud service providers serving overseas markets via Indian data centres.
However, a new rule requiring cloud services for Indian users to go through Indian resellers could discourage investors by interfering with commercial business models.
analysis.what_happened: India wants to become a global hub for data centres (large facilities that store and process internet data) and artificial intelligence. To attract big global tech companies, the Ministry of Finance introduced tax incentives, but experts warn that overlapping rules and tricky conditions might hold investors back unless laws become more predictable.
analysis.analogy: It is like opening a mega-restaurant: having hungry customers isn't enough if you have to get separate licenses from twenty different government windows just to turn on the stove.
why_it_matters_india: Clearer regulations and tax incentives -> global tech giants invest heavily in Indian data infrastructure
More data centres built -> higher demand for domestic power, real estate, and digital hardware
Better digital infrastructure -> stronger growth for cloud computing and AI-driven services in India
Consistent policy -> foreign investors feel safer bringing long-term capital into the country

impacts.target: Technology stocks (like TCS, Infosys, and telecom/cloud players)
impacts.rationale: Clearer data centre policies could drive more digital infrastructure business to Indian tech firms — generally good for tech investors.

impacts.target: Foreign capital inflows (money coming from foreign investors)
impacts.rationale: Predictable tax laws and regulations encourage foreign companies to invest billions in Indian infrastructure — good for the broader economy.

watch_next: How the government writes the final subordinate regulations for the 21-year tax carve-out
Whether rules forcing foreign cloud providers to use local resellers are changed or relaxed
analysis.caveats: If overzealous enforcement or restrictive reseller rules are upheld, foreign investors may choose other global destinations instead of India.

events.headline: CEA flags US friction, energy shocks, and missing AI play as India’s key near-term risks

items.title: CEA flags US friction, energy shocks, and missing AI play as India’s key near-term risks
items.summary: CEA V. Anantha Nageswaran warned that trade coercion, weaponized supply chains, and rising US bond yields require India to adopt a costlier hedging strategy and a new economic playbook.

events.article_text:
New Delhi: Chief economic advisor V Anantha Nageswaran on Friday flagged unsettled relations with the US, disruptions in the energy market and the absence of the so-called artificial intelligence (AI) play as three near-term headwinds for India.

US tariffs, the new law seeking to punish Russian oil importers, and trade curbs could be seen as a part of "sustained coercion for countries to choose between the blocs”, Nageswaran said at an event of the Public Affairs Forum of India. Capital inflows into India, especially foreign portfolio inflows, could be impacted due to the unsettled relations with the US, he said.

"Given its location, size and geography, India cannot afford to choose. The answer is therefore hedging,” he said, cautioning that hedging will cost much more, which is something both the public and private sectors must factor into their decision-making.

Last week, the US passed a law empowering President Donald Trump to impose up to 100% tariffs on key countries buying Russian oil, including India and China. To be sure, the power to decide whether to impose fresh tariffs or not, and at what rate and on what products, lies with Trump.

India has been engaged in talks with the US to seal a trade deal—a point commerce and industry minister Piyush Goyal reiterated on Thursday. A trade pact between India and the US is "done and dusted", Goyal said. It will be sealed once the US gives India the right competitive edge over its competitors. The US was India’s biggest export market in 2026-27, accounting for goods supplies worth $87 billion.

The CEA also said that rising bond yields in advanced economies will make investors less willing to send capital to emerging markets, and "there will be pressure on capital mobilisation for a while”.

Pointing to the rise in US interest rates in the past few days, the CEA added that India’s garnering of dollars through the foreign currency non-resident (FCNR-B) deposits was well-timed. “If we were mopping the FCNR deposits now, we wouldn’t have got what we have got in the previous three months after this kind of interest rate increase (in the US). So, in a way, it was a fortuitous case of timing,” he added.

The US’s 10-year Treasury yields have shot up 102 basis points so far this year to 5.19%, including 25 basis points in the past three days. Any increase in the US rates narrows the gap with Indian rates and reduces the appeal of the Indian instruments.

India drew a record $127 billion in FCNR bank deposits under the RBI’s special forex swap facility between June 8 and August 31. The central bank’s three measures—a special forex swap facility for FCNR bank deposits, overseas foreign currency borrowings (OFCB) and external commercial borrowings (ECBs)—led to total inflows of $136 billion over this period. The steps were taken to bolster India’s external sector position and support foreign exchange liquidity amid mounting external headwinds.

Pointing to an increasingly difficult geopolitical and economic backdrop for India’s Viksit Bharat 2047 vision, Nageswaran advocated a fundamental rethink of the roles played by the public and private sectors. The 1980-2020 playbook is no longer valid, and the current global stress isn’t stemming from demand but supply shocks, he said. “Geopolitics is different now. Economic choke points are weaponized, globalization won’t supply goods whenever, wherever and in whatever quantities we need them, and the prices are higher,” he said.

The huge manufacturing scale of China poses challenges for other countries to grow their manufacturing prowess and employment, he added. But India must invest in manufacturing because an increasingly protectionist world won’t ensure steady supply of goods at reasonable rates. “That’s the dilemma and the exacting challenge that we face,” Nageswaran said.

analysis.tldr: Rising global interest rates and US trade pressures could make it harder for foreign money to enter India, forcing businesses and the government to spend more on protecting themselves.
the_story: Chief Economic Advisor V Anantha Nageswaran flagged US relations, energy disruptions, and missing AI capabilities as three near-term risks for India.
The US recently passed a law allowing the president to impose up to 100% tariffs on countries like India and China that buy Russian oil.
US 10-year Treasury yields (the interest rate the US government pays to borrow) have shot up by 102 basis points this year to 5.19%.
India previously secured $127 billion in FCNR-B (foreign currency non-resident) bank deposits under a special central bank facility, which the CEA called well-timed given the current rate hikes.
analysis.what_happened: India's top economic advisor warned that global tensions, potential US tariffs on Russian oil buyers, and rising borrowing costs in developed countries are creating major economic hurdles. These global shifts make it more expensive and difficult to attract foreign money, forcing India to rely more on its own manufacturing and defensive strategies.
analysis.analogy: It is like trying to borrow money from a bank when your local lender suddenly raises its interest rates; suddenly, everyone prefers to keep their cash with the lender paying higher rates rather than lending to you.
why_it_matters_india: US bond yields rise as global interest rates climb -> Foreign investors pull money back to safer US markets instead of sending it to emerging countries like India -> Foreign investments and portfolio inflows into India face mounting pressure.

Potential US trade curbs and tariffs on Russian oil create friction -> Businesses must spend more money on hedging (protecting themselves against currency and trade shocks) -> Overall corporate and public sector costs go up.

Global manufacturing becomes more protectionist (countries prioritizing themselves) -> Supply chains get disrupted and goods become pricier -> India faces the dual challenge of building local manufacturing while navigating expensive global markets.

impacts.target: Foreign portfolio inflows (money from big foreign investors into Indian stocks and bonds)
impacts.rationale: Higher US interest rates make safe US assets more attractive, leading foreign investors to pull funds from emerging markets like India—generally bad for local market liquidity.
Stiff trade friction and slowing capital inflows put downward pressure on India's currency, making imported items like crude oil more expensive for regular people.

watch_next: Updates on US trade deals and potential tariff announcements concerning Russian oil imports
Further movements in US 10-year Treasury yields
analysis.caveats: The impact of potential US tariffs depends entirely on whether and how the US administration chooses to enforce the newly passed laws.

events.headline: Nifty slips below 23,000 as bank stocks tumble

items.title: Nifty slips below 23,000 as bank stocks tumble
items.summary: The key equity benchmarks remained under pressure in the early afternoon session on Monday, weighed down by weak global cues, rising crude oil prices and weakness in global technology stocks amid concerns over the reliability and safety of AI agents. The Nifty traded below the 23,000 level.

events.article_text:
The key equity benchmarks remained under pressure in the early afternoon session on Monday, weighed down by weak global cues, rising crude oil prices and weakness in global technology stocks amid concerns over the reliability and safety of AI agents. The Nifty traded below the 23,000 level.

Investors remained focused on crude oil price movements, developments in the primary market and upcoming initial public offerings (IPOs). A series of domestic and global economic data releases due during the week are also expected to influence market expectations around monetary policy decisions by central banks.

At 12:25 IST, the S&P BSE Sensex was down 917.53 points, or 1.24%, at 72,978.21. The Nifty 50 index was down 292.35 points, or 1.26%, at 22,848.15.

ICICI Bank (down 1.68%), Max Healthcare Institute (down 1.08%) and Bharti Airtel (down 0.56%%) were major Nifty drags.

In the broader market, the Nifty Midcap 100 index fell 1.24%. The Nifty Smallcap 100 index fell 1.35%.

On the NSE, 825 shares were trading in green, while 2599 shares were trading in red. A total of 83 shares were unchanged.

The NSE's India VIX, which gauges expected near-term market volatility, jumped 13.19% to 13.77.

The Nifty 27 October 2026 futures traded at 22,952.10, a premium of 103.95 points over the spot level of 22,848.15.

The Nifty option chain for the 27 October 2026 expiry showed maximum call open interest of 44,058 contracts at the 23,000 strike, while maximum put open interest stood at 42,942 contracts at the 22,000 strike.

The Nifty Bank index fell 1.81% to 54576.9. Yes Bank (down 4.44%), Union Bank of India (down 3.39%), IDFC First Bank (down 2.88%), Punjab National Bank (down 2.74%) and Canara Bank (down 2.66%) were the top losers. Among the other losers were Bank of Baroda (down 2.41%), IndusInd Bank (down 1.93%), HDFC Bank (down 1.86%), AU Small Finance Bank (down 1.85%) and State Bank of India (down 1.83%) declined.

Silver Touch Technologies added 1.9% after the company announced the receipt of a purchase order from the Space Applications Centre (SAC), ISRO, for the supply of high-end workstations.

Disclaimer: No Business Standard Journalist was involved in creation of this content

Don't miss the most important news and views of the day. Get them on our Telegram channel

analysis.tldr: When the share market drops sharply like this, the paper wealth of everyday investors shrinks and borrowing costs or future loan rates can feel the ripple effect.
the_story: The Nifty 50 index fell 292.35 points (1.26%) to trade below 23,000, settling at 22,848.15 by early afternoon on Monday.
The S&P BSE Sensex dropped 917.53 points (1.24%) to 72,978.21, dragged down by weak global markets, rising crude oil prices, and falling global technology stocks over AI safety concerns.
Major banking stocks suffered heavy losses, with the Nifty Bank index down 1.81% and individual lenders like Yes Bank dropping 4.44% and Union Bank falling 3.39%.
The NSE's India VIX (a gauge of expected near-term market volatility or nervousness) jumped 13.19% to 13.77.
Silver Touch Technologies gained 1.9% after winning a purchase order from the Space Applications Centre (SAC), ISRO, for high-end workstations.
analysis.what_happened: Indian share markets dropped sharply because global markets were weak, crude oil prices rose, and international tech stocks slumped due to worries over artificial intelligence tools. This global negativity made investors cautious, leading to widespread selling in Indian banks and other major companies.
analysis.analogy: It is like a crowded cricket stadium where one person suddenly shouts that it is going to rain, causing everyone in the stands to rush for the exit at the same time and stumble over each other.
why_it_matters_india: Weak global cues and rising crude oil prices lower investor confidence in India.
Traders sell off heavyweights like bank stocks, pulling down major indexes like the Nifty 50 and Sensex below key psychological levels.
Market nervousness surges, reflected by a sharp jump in the volatility index.
Overall portfolio values for everyday mutual fund and stock investors temporarily shrink.

impacts.rationale: Fell 1.26% due to selling pressure, which is generally unsettling for everyday investors tracking their mutual funds.

impacts.target: India VIX (market fear and volatility gauge)
impacts.rationale: Jumped 13.19%, signaling that traders expect bumpy and unpredictable stock movements ahead — usually an uncomfortable sign for regular investors.
Fell 1.81% as major lenders like Yes Bank, Union Bank, and SBI saw heavy selling, pulling down banking sector wealth.

watch_next: Upcoming domestic and global economic data releases
Primary market developments and upcoming initial public offerings (IPOs)
analysis.caveats: Markets can quickly reverse course if global cues or upcoming economic data turn out better than expected.

items.title: Federal Reserve Board issues enforcement actions with former employee of Northstar Bank, former employee of American Express Travel Related Services Company, Inc., and former employee of Regions Bank
items.summary: Federal Reserve Board issues enforcement actions with former employee of Northstar Bank, former employee of American Express Travel Related Services Company, Inc., and former employee of Regions Bank

analysis.tldr: This US banking news is about local employee fraud cases and has no direct impact on your daily expenses, the rupee, or Indian markets.
the_story: The Federal Reserve Board (the US central bank) announced enforcement actions against three former employees from different US financial institutions on Friday.
Charles Alan Wright, a former employee of Northstar Bank in Bad Axe, Michigan, faced a consent prohibition order for misappropriation of customer funds.
Stephanie K. Hudders, a former employee of American Express Travel Related Services Company, Inc. in New York, faced an order for misapplication of funds and conflicts of interest.
Elvisha White, a former employee of Regions Bank in Birmingham, Alabama, faced an order for check fraud.
analysis.what_happened: The US Federal Reserve issued bans (called consent prohibition orders) stopping three former bank employees from ever working in the US banking industry again, because they committed fraud or misused customer and company funds at their respective institutions.
analysis.analogy: It is like three rogue employees getting permanently banned from ever working in a bank again after being caught stealing from the cash register.
why_it_matters_india: The news involves specific local US bank employees committing internal fraud.
There are no macroeconomic changes, interest rate adjustments, or broad financial policy shifts mentioned.
Because this is an isolated US regulatory housekeeping matter, it does not alter global financial flows.
Therefore, there is no transmission channel to Indian inflation, currency markets, or local stock prices.

impacts.rationale: Local US bank employee disciplinary actions have no bearing on Indian corporate earnings or stock prices.
Currency values move based on macro factors like trade and interest rates, not individual US bank employee bans.

watch_next: Broader US Federal Reserve interest rate announcements that actually impact global markets
analysis.caveats: This is purely an administrative legal notice about US domestic banking misconduct with zero connection to the Indian economy.

events.headline: China’s Gwadar gamble isn’t paying off

items.title: China’s Gwadar gamble isn’t paying off
items.summary: An attempted shortcut around the Malacca Strait has left a port without profit or security.

events.article_text:
A view of the Gwadar port, part of the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor, linking Gwadar port with Kashgar in northwest China. and a flagship project under Belt and Road Initiative (Ahmad Kamal/Xinhua via Getty Images)

An attempted shortcut around the Malacca Strait has left a port without profit or security.

The Gwadar Port (Opens in new window), the crown jewel of the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC) (Opens in new window) and hero of the Belt and Road Initiative, now looks like a monument to strategic overreach. Once hailed as China’s ultimate maritime shortcut to bypass the treacherous Malacca Strait (Opens in new window), the deep-sea port is rapidly transforming from a geopolitical asset into a financial and security liability as Beijing’s risk appetite diminishes under domestic economic strain (Opens in new window).

The core premise of Gwadar was to connect China’s landlocked western province of Xinjiang (Opens in new window) directly to the Arabian Sea (Opens in new window). However, the physical and geopolitical terrain through which this trade must traverse makes it one of the most perilous logistical corridors in the world.

Goods moving from Xinjiang to Gwadar must cross the Karakoram highway (Opens in new window), navigating altitudes of over 4,600 metres. The area is plagued by frequent landslides, avalanches, and extreme weather, rendering it structurally incapable of handling the high-volume container traffic required to replace maritime shipping.

Once past the mountains, the route cuts through Gilgit-Baltistan (Opens in new window), Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (Opens in new window), and Balochistan (Opens in new window). Convoys must pass through territories marked by intense sectarian violence, Taliban activity (Opens in new window), and deep-seated local insurgencies.

Infrastructure abounds, but commercial opportunities are yet to follow (Ahmad Kamal/Xinhua via Getty Images)

Gwadar sits in Balochistan, Pakistan’s most volatile province. The Baloch Liberation Army (Opens in new window) (BLA) and other insurgent groups view CPEC as an imperialist exploitation of their natural resources. Consequently, Chinese engineering units, convoys, and infrastructure have become primary targets for sophisticated suicide bombings and guerrilla ambushes.

The BLA’s specialised Majeed Brigade (Opens in new window) has shifted from low-intensity guerrilla skirmishes to high-yield suicide strikes explicitly aimed at maximising Chinese casualties. The frequency of these incidents has strained the “Iron Brother” relationship between Islamabad and Beijing. It has forced Pakistan to raise dedicated Special Security Divisions (SSD) (Opens in new window), which are still failing to completely shield Chinese infrastructure from asymmetric threats.

China originally saw Gwadar as a chance to solve its “Malacca Dilemma (Opens in new window)” – the fear that the US Navy could blockade the narrow Malacca Strait during a conflict, choking China’s energy imports. Mechanically and economically, Gwadar fails to solve this problem.

Pipelines and overland trucking are exponentially more expensive than ocean freight. Pumping oil upward through thousands of kilometres of mountainous terrain from Gwadar to Xinjiang requires immense energy, destroying the commercial viability of the route. A pipeline or railway stretching 3,000 kilometres through hostile Pakistani territory is impossible to secure. It represents a massive, static target for sabotage. Even if oil lands at Gwadar, tankers must still cross the Indian Ocean, where the Indian Navy holds dominant positions.

China is growing weary of sacrificing both capital and the lives of its citizens to defend a commercial failure.

For a mega-infrastructure project to succeed, it requires a baseline of local political stability. In Gwadar, China and the Pakistani state have achieved the exact opposite by completely alienating the local populace. The local Baloch population has been excluded from the economic benefits of the port. Massive, prolonged civil protests led by the Haq Do Tehreek (Opens in new window) (Give Rights Movement) have repeatedly shut down the port area. The high-tech jobs are given to Chinese expatriates, while the low-skilled labour is largely brought in from Pakistan’s Punjab province. While millions are spent on port infrastructure, the city of Gwadar suffers from acute shortages (Opens in new window) of drinking water and electricity. The local fishing community – the backbone of the regional economy – has been displaced (Opens in new window) by Chinese deep-sea trawlers and security exclusion zones.

The economic architecture supporting CPEC is fundamentally broken. Pakistan is trapped in a structural balance-of-payments crisis, relying on rolling IMF bailouts and Chinese debt deferrals to avoid sovereign default.

A port requires a bustling industrial hinterland to survive. The Special Economic Zones planned around Gwadar remain largely empty shells. Major international shipping lines continue to bypass Gwadar in favour of established regional hubs such as Dubai, Salalah, or even Karachi, because Gwadar lacks the cargo volume to justify docking.

China has poured billions into Gwadar, but under the current 40-year lease, 91% of the port’s revenues are supposed (Opens in new window) to go to Beijing. Because the port generates virtually no revenue, China is extracting no returns (Opens in new window) while forced to spend heavily to secure its stranded assets. Indeed, China’s own economic slowdown has led to the tightening of capital controls and a shift away from high-risk, high-cost overseas megaprojects. Beijing is transitioning from the expansive “Belt and Road (Opens in new window)” era to a more cautious “small is beautiful” development framework. Gwadar’s massive maintenance costs are becoming indefensible to Chinese state planners.

Gwadar is rapidly approaching a tipping point. Pakistan cannot afford to secure or maintain i

analysis.tldr: China's struggle with its expensive Pakistan port highlights regional instability, keeping India's northern maritime trade routes strategically secure.
the_story: The Gwadar Port, part of the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC) and the Belt and Road Initiative, is failing to turn a profit or provide secure trade for China.
China built Gwadar as a shortcut to bypass the Malacca Strait, but moving goods from Xinjiang across the 4,600-meter-high Karakoram highway is too costly and plagued by extreme weather.
The route passes through violent regions like Balochistan, where local insurgent groups like the Baloch Liberation Army and its Majeed Brigade target Chinese engineers and infrastructure.
The local Baloch population has been alienated by job exclusion and water/electricity shortages, leading to major civil protests by the Haq Do Tehreek.
Under a 40-year lease, 91% of port revenues go to Beijing, but the port generates virtually no money while requiring massive security and maintenance costs.
analysis.what_happened: China's flagship Gwadar Port project in Pakistan has turned into a financial and security failure because of extreme mountain terrain, fierce local insurgent attacks, and bitter protests by local residents. China is cutting back on risky overseas megaprojects due to its own domestic economic slowdown.
analysis.analogy: It is like buying an expensive sports car as a shortcut to work, only to find the road is constantly blocked by landslides, local thugs keep damaging the car, and it costs more in repairs than your salary.
why_it_matters_india: China's grand trade route through Pakistan faces heavy security and financial roadblocks.
Because the port and overland routes are too dangerous and expensive, China cannot easily use them to bypass maritime shipping lanes.
This reduces long-term military encirclement pressures from Pakistan-based Chinese infrastructure near India's western maritime approaches.
It keeps regional shipping focused on established hubs rather than a hostile military-commercial choke point near the Indian Ocean.

impacts.rationale: Geopolitical friction in Pakistan has a very minor indirect effect on broad Indian stock markets.

watch_next: Future Chinese funding announcements for Belt and Road Initiative projects
Security updates on the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC)
analysis.caveats: This report is based entirely on the published article analysis of Gwadar's current challenges.

events.headline: Tariffs applied by WTO members have decreased by a third since 1996

items.title: Tariffs applied by WTO members have decreased by a third since 1996
items.summary: Update of data blog first published on 13 April 2023.

events.article_text:
By Monia Snoussi-Mimouni and Edvinas Drevinskas

Update of data blog first published on 13 April 2023.

There has been a clear downward trend in tariffs since the WTO was established in 1995.

Since 1996, global trade in goods has more than quadrupled, reaching a total of US$ 20.1 trillion for imports in 2024, compared to US$ 4.6 trillion in 1996.

Over the same period, available data indicate that the simple average tariff applied by WTO members on a most-favoured nation basis - by which WTO members extend the same trade treatment, including tariff rates and market access, to all other members - has declined by 32 per cent, falling from 13.1 per cent to 8.9 per cent, as shown in Figure 1.

A similar trend emerges for tariffs applied on a trade-weighted basis, with the average MFN tariff dropping from 7.0 per cent to 3.9 per cent.

Taking into account preferential tariff regimes, including those offered by developed countries to developing and least-developed economies, and those in regional trade agreements (RTAs), an even steeper decline is visible. Between 1996 and 2024, the trade-weighted average of effective applied tariffs - based on the assumption of full utilization of preferential tariffs - dropped from 6.8 per cent to 2.2 per cent. The reason for this larger decrease was the increased trade in products subject to lower tariffs.

Figure 2 illustrates changes by product group between 1996 and 2024. Notably, the tariffs on agricultural products declined more than those of industrial products, which were already low in 1996. For example, the largest decrease in trade-weighted MFN applied tariffs on agricultural goods were observed for: oilseeds, fats and oils; cereals and preparation; and animal products. The tariffs for each of these categories fell by about 50 per cent between 1996 and 2024, while the largest decrease in tariffs on industrial goods was for electrical machinery which declined from 5.1 per cent in 1996 to 1.4 per cent in 2024.

The changes in trade-weighted averages could be attributed not only to changes in tariffs, but also to changes in trade flows. For instance, an increase in trade in goods combined with a lower tariff within a product group will result in a decrease in the trade-weighted average.

These figures cover the period up to 2024 and do not yet reflect tariff measures introduced since 2025. Despite recent trade policy uncertainty, 72 per cent of world trade in 2026 continues to be conducted on MFN terms. It is difficult to predict the future direction of tariffs as a range of factors can influence WTO members' actions. However, the WTO remains committed to helping its members ensure that trade flows as smoothly, predictably and freely as possible.

analysis.tldr: Global import taxes have dropped significantly over the past decades, making it cheaper for countries to buy and sell goods across borders, which generally helps export-focused businesses thrive.
the_story: Since 1996, global trade in goods has more than quadrupled, reaching a total of US$ 20.1 trillion for imports in 2024, up from US$ 4.6 trillion in 1996.

The simple average tariff [tax on imports] applied by World Trade Organization members on a most-favoured nation basis [a rule where countries treat all trading partners equally without special favors] has dropped by 32 per cent, falling from 13.1 per cent to 8.9 per cent.
Tariffs on agricultural products [farm goods] declined more than industrial products, with taxes on oilseeds, fats and oils, cereals, and animal products falling by about 50 per cent.
For industrial goods, the largest decrease was seen in electrical machinery, where tariffs dropped from 5.1 per cent in 1996 to 1.4 per cent in 2024.
Despite recent trade policy uncertainty, 72 per cent of world trade in 2026 continues to be conducted on these equal-treatment MFN terms.
analysis.what_happened: Data published by the World Trade Organization shows that global import taxes have steadily decreased since 1995. This happened as countries traded more goods overall and shifted toward product categories with lower taxes, especially in farming and electrical machinery.
analysis.analogy: It is like a local market where shopkeepers slowly lower their entry fees over the years, making it much easier and cheaper for vendors from different towns to bring and sell their goods.
why_it_matters_india: Lower global tariffs -> Cheaper movement of goods across international borders -> Indian exporters find it easier to sell agricultural and electrical goods abroad
Rising global trade volume -> Greater demand for international shipping and manufactured parts -> Boosts revenues for Indian manufacturing and export companies
Broader global market access -> Indian companies face less expensive tax barriers -> Can help expand profit margins for export-oriented businesses
However, the data only covers up to 2024 and does not reflect newer tariff measures introduced since 2025

impacts.rationale: Lower historical trade barriers globally create a supportive environment for export-heavy companies, which is generally good for overall stock market sentiment.
Smoother global trade and economic growth generally encourage businesses worldwide to spend more on technology services.

watch_next: New tariff measures and trade policy changes introduced since 2025
Future updates from the World Trade Organization on global trade flows
analysis.caveats: The reported figures cover historical data up to 2024 and do not yet reflect newer trade policy uncertainties or tariff measures introduced since 2025.

history.title: Most of a country's cash cancelled overnight
history.what: At 8pm on 8 November, ₹500 and ₹1,000 notes — about 86% of India's currency by value — ceased to be legal tender at midnight. Queues formed outside banks for weeks.
history.why: The stated aims were to destroy unaccounted wealth, counterfeit notes and terror financing. The underlying logic was that illicit cash hoards would simply never be deposited, and would therefore be extinguished.
history.impact: Nearly 99% of the cancelled notes came back into the banking system, so the black-money aim largely failed. But the cash-dependent informal economy — small traders, daily-wage labour, farm markets — was badly disrupted, and growth slowed for several quarters.
history.policy: What followed mattered far more than the disruption itself. Digital payments were pushed hard: UPI, launched months earlier, was given enormous impetus, and bank account penetration jumped.
history.consequence: India now runs the largest real-time payments system in the world by volume. Household savings shifted out of cash and gold and into bank deposits and mutual funds — the beginning of the monthly SIP flows that now support the Indian equity market. Almost nobody predicted that from the announcement.
history.pattern: A policy's stated aim and its lasting effect are often different things, and the lasting effect usually comes from the infrastructure built around it. Judge policies by what they permanently changed, not by whether they hit their stated target.
history.india_echo: The monthly SIP flow that cushions every Nifty selloff traces partly back to this. It is the clearest case on this list of a disruptive policy producing a durable change in where Indian savings go.
history.watch_for: Infrastructure being laid alongside a policy. The rails usually outlive the reason they were built.
